public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 269

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/269](https://www.erdosproblems.com/269)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos269
/--
A positive integer $n$ has all its prime factors in the set $P$.
By convention, $1$ satisfies this for any $P$ as it has no prime divisors.
-/
def HasPrimeFactorsIn (P : Set ℕ) (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  n > 0 ∧ ∀ p, p.Prime → p ∣ n → p ∈ P

/--
The infinite, strictly increasing sequence $\{a_0, a_1, \dots\}$ of integers
whose prime factors all belong to $P$.
-/
noncomputable def a (P : Set ℕ) : ℕ → ℕ := Nat.nth <| HasPrimeFactorsIn P

/--
The $n$-th partial least common multiple, $[a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}]$, which is
the LCM of the first $n$ integers in the sequence.
-/
noncomputable def partialLcm (P : Set ℕ) (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  -- We take the LCM of `{a P 0, ..., a P n}`.
  (Finset.range n).lcm (a P)

/--
The sum $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{[a_0,\ldots,a_{n - 1}]}$.
-/
noncomputable def series (P : Set ℕ) : ℝ :=  ∑' n, (1 : ℝ) / (partialLcm P n)

/--
Let $P$ be a finite set of primes with $|P| \ge 2$ and let
$\{a_1 < a_2 < \dots\}$ be the set of positive integers whose prime factors
are all in $P$. Is the sum
$$ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{[a_1,\ldots,a_n]} $$
rational?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_269.variants.rational : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ᵉ (P : Finset ℕ) (h : ∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) (h_card : P.card ≥ 2),
    ∃ (q : ℚ), q = (series (P : Set ℕ)) := by
  sorry

/--
Let $P$ be a finite set of primes with $|P| \ge 2$ and let
$\{a_1 < a_2 < \dots\}$ be the set of positive integers whose prime factors
are all in $P$. Is the sum
$$ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{[a_1,\ldots,a_n]} $$
irrational?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_269.variants.irrational : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ᵉ (P : Finset ℕ) (h : ∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) (h_card : P.card ≥ 2),
    Irrational (series (P : Set ℕ)) := by
  sorry

/--
This theorem addresses the case where the set of primes $P$ is infinite. In this case the sum is
irrational.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_269.variants.infinite (P : Set ℕ) (h : ∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) (h_inf : P.Infinite) :
  Irrational (series P) := by
  sorry

end Erdos269

findings.description: The statement elaborates to `answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ P : Finset ℕ, (∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) → P.card ≥ 2 → ∃ q : ℚ, ↑q = series ↑P`, i.e. "for EVERY finite set P of at least two primes the sum is rational". The source asks only whether the sum is irrational, and `variants.irrational` already states that question faithfully. This variant is neither the source's question nor its negation. The negation of `∀ P, Irrational (series P)` is `∃ P, (∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) ∧ 2 ≤ P.card ∧ series P ∈ ℚ`, but this variant quantifies universally. So it is NOT a negated conjecture, and the two answer slots do not simply invert. If S(P) is rational for some P and irrational for others, the source's answer is 'no' (so the inverted answer would be 'yes'), yet this right-hand side is false. More concretely, the forum proof that S(P) is transcendental whenever |P| = 2 would make this right-hand side false (answer False) while Erdős's question, which is still open for |P| ≥ 3, stays unsettled. So this variant can be 'solved' without answering the source's problem. Its docstring attributes 'Is the sum … rational?' to the source, which never asks this. This matters in practice: `FormalConjectures/Subsets/FC100OpenSet1.lean` (line 208) lists exactly `Erdos269.erdos_269.variants.rational` as the open problem for Erdős 269, counted among its 85 'research open' items.
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/269, LaTeX source (https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/269): 'Let $P$ be a finite set of primes with $\lvert P\rvert \geq 2$ and let $\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}=\{ n\in \mathbb{N} : \textrm{if }p\mid n\textrm{ then }p\in P\}$. Is the sum $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{[a_1,\ldots,a_n]}$ ... irrational?' Erdős [Er88c, p.106] (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1988-22.pdf): for an infinite sequence of primes, irrationality is 'a simple exercise ... This result probably remains true if the number of primes p_i is finite but of course greater than 1.' No source asks whether the sum is always rational. Forum (https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/discuss/269, Steve Fan, 26 Jun 2026): 'Here is a short proof of the case |P|=2, which actually shows that S is transcendental ... This argument does not seem to generalize immediately to |P| ≥ 3'.
findings.suggested_fix: Delete `erdos_269.variants.rational`, rename `erdos_269.variants.irrational` to the main `erdos_269`, and update FC100OpenSet1 to reference `Erdos269.erdos_269`. If a rationality-phrased statement is wanted, it must be the negation: `answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ P : Finset ℕ, (∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) ∧ 2 ≤ P.card ∧ ∃ q : ℚ, (q : ℝ) = series P`.

findings.description: The docstring says `series P` is '$\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{[a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1}]}$'. But the Lean `∑' n, (1 : ℝ) / partialLcm P n` runs over every n : ℕ, including n = 0. That term is 1/((Finset.range 0).lcm (a P)) = 1/1 = 1 (`Finset.lcm_empty`). So `series P` equals the docstring's sum plus 1, i.e. 1 + the source's ∑_{n≥1} 1/[a_1,…,a_n]. For P = {2,3} that is ≈ 2.932950 instead of ≈ 1.932950. The code comment inside `partialLcm` ('the LCM of `{a P 0, ..., a P n}`') is also off by one: it is the LCM of a P 0, …, a P (n−1). No theorem is affected, because adding the rational number 1 preserves rationality and irrationality (proved in Lean; see reformulations).
findings.source_evidence: The source's sum is '∑_{n=1}^∞ 1/[a_1,…,a_n]' with a_1 = 1 (https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/269). In Lean, `example (P : Set ℕ) : partialLcm P 0 = 1 := by simp [partialLcm]` and `partialLcm P 1 = 1` (using `a P 0 = 1`) both compile. Numerically, the source sum for P = {2,3} is ≈ 1.932950.
findings.suggested_fix: Define `series P := ∑' n, (1 : ℝ) / partialLcm P (n + 1)` so that it is literally the source's sum. Alternatively, change the docstring to a sum from n = 0 and note the extra leading term 1/[∅] = 1. Also fix the comment to `{a P 0, ..., a P (n - 1)}`.

status_issues.source_status: The problem page still says OPEN, because the question for all |P| ≥ 2 is unresolved (|P| ≥ 3 open). But the page's comment thread contains a proof (Steve Fan, 26 Jun 2026) that the sum is transcendental for every P with |P| = 2. If correct, this variant's right-hand side (∀ P, S(P) ∈ ℚ) is false (take P = {2,3}), so its answer is False.
status_issues.evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/discuss/269: 'Here is a short proof of the case |P| = 2, which actually shows that S is transcendental.' The argument: S = S₁S₂; (p−1)S₁ + (q−1)S₂ = p+q−1; S₂ = 1/(q−1) − (p−1)F_β(1/q,1/p) + 1 with β = log q/log p; and transcendence of the Hecke–Mahler series F_β. A later comment (williamwkcook, 11 Sep 2026) credits 'the two-prime factorisation, Hecke–Mahler reduction and transcendence conclusion' to Fan. I checked the reduction numerically for P = {2,3}: S ≈ 1.932950 = S₁·S₂ (S₁ ≈ 1.633803, S₂ ≈ 1.183098), and (p−1)S₁ + (q−1)S₂ = 4.000000 = p+q−1.
status_issues.suggested_change: Preferably delete the variant (see the finding). If it is kept, change it to `@[category research solved]` with `answer(False)` and cite the forum proof. The faithful `variants.irrational` correctly stays `research open`.

reformulations.difference: All three theorems (`variants.rational`, `variants.irrational`, `variants.infinite`) are stated about `series P = ∑_{n≥0} 1/lcm(a P 0,…,a P (n−1))`. Here `a P` is 0-indexed with a P 0 = 1, and the n = 0 term is 1/lcm(∅) = 1. So `series P` = 1 + the source's ∑_{n≥1} 1/[a_1,…,a_n], not the source's sum itself.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every theorem's hypotheses (card ≥ 2, or P infinite) give two distinct primes p ≠ q in P. The prime powers p^{⌊log_p a_n⌋} and q^{⌊log_q a_n⌋} are P-smooth and ≤ a_n, so they are among a_0..a_n. Being coprime, their product divides partialLcm P (n+1), and it exceeds a_n²/(pq) ≥ (n+1)²/(pq). Hence the series is summable and the tsum is the genuine sum, never the junk value 0. Then series P = 1 + ∑' n, 1/partialLcm P (n+1) = 1 + S(P), and x ↦ 1 + x preserves both rationality and irrationality. So each right-hand side is equivalent to the same statement with the source's S(P). Whether 1 counts among Erdős's 'integers composed of the p's' also only shifts the sum by 1, so that convention is immaterial as well. Proved in Lean with no sorry (axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound) in /workspace/review/summable.lean: `summable_series`, `irrational_rhs_iff`, `rational_rhs_iff`, `infinite_iff`.

https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1988-22.pdf — P. Erdős, On the irrationality of certain series: problems and results, New advances in transcendence theory (1988), p.106 (text read via r.jina.ai)

The status point on Erdos269.erdos_269.variants.rational depends on an unrefereed forum proof for |P| = 2. That proof uses the classical transcendence of Hecke–Mahler series F_θ(α,β) for irrational θ and algebraic α, β (Mahler; Loxton–van der Poorten). I checked its algebraic reduction numerically, but could not consult the transcendence literature (arXiv API rate-limited).
review.notes: The file has no main `erdos_269` declaration. `erdos_269.variants.irrational` is the faithful statement of the source's question: its `answer(sorry)` polarity is correct and its 'research open' tag matches the source. `erdos_269.variants.infinite` faithfully states the source's remark that the sum is irrational for infinite P, and 'research solved' is appropriate ([Er88c] calls it 'a simple exercise'; there is also a forum proof by Steve Fan, Oct 2025). `HasPrimeFactorsIn` correctly includes 1 and excludes 0. `a P` is the 0-indexed enumeration with a P 0 = 1 (proved). All three theorems reach only P with at least two primes, so the series is always summable (proved in Lean) and no junk tsum value arises. Under the default `google.answer` option, `answer(sorry) : Prop` elaborates to `True` (`#print` shows `True ↔ …`); that is tooling only. The erdosproblems.com edit history (from 2025-10-20) shows only a comma change, so I could not see whether the page's wording differed when the file was written (the database records it as formalized on 2025-09-02). The Wayback Machine was unreachable from the sandbox. Scratch files: /workspace/review/scratch2.lean (boundary values, series = 1 + S given summability) and /workspace/review/summable.lean (summability and the three ↔ equivalences, all sorry-free).

not_demonstrated.reason: The defect is that the variant asks a different question from the source: 'always rational', which is not the negation of Erdős's 'always irrational?'. Whether that question's answer is True or False is itself unknown without deep mathematics. A disproof needs the irrationality of `Erdos269.series` for some P with |P| ≥ 2 (only known via the Hecke–Mahler transcendence argument for |P| = 2). Showing that it differs from the negated conjecture needs knowledge of which P give rational sums, which nobody has. `series P` is a genuine convergent sum (summability proved separately), so no Lean junk value gives a short proof or disproof.

submission.summary: No trivial demonstration is possible. Erdos269.erdos_269.variants.rational states "∀ P, series P is rational", a question the source never asks and which is not the negation of its irrationality question. Its truth is unknown without deep mathematics: refuting it needs the Hecke–Mahler transcendence argument for |P| = 2, and showing it differs from the negated conjecture needs knowledge of which sums are rational, which nobody has. The series is genuinely summable (proved earlier), so there is no junk-value shortcut. No trivial_proof.lean file was created.
submission.gave_up_reason: The only reported misformalization, Erdos269.erdos_269.variants.rational, poses a different question from the source: "∀ P (finite, ≥ 2 primes), series P ∈ ℚ". That is neither Erdős's irrationality question nor its negation "∃ P, series P ∈ ℚ". Its truth value is unknown without real mathematics. (1) Refuting it needs Irrational (series P) for some P with |P| ≥ 2. The only known route is the forum's argument that the sum is transcendental for |P| = 2, which uses the classical transcendence theorem for Hecke–Mahler series (Mahler; Loxton–van der Poorten); that is far from a few lines. (2) Proving it is presumably impossible, since the same argument makes it false. (3) Showing it is not equivalent to the negated conjecture would need one P with a rational sum and one with an irrational sum, which nobody knows. The easy lemma "RHS_rational → ¬RHS_irrational" fits complementarity and shows no defect. (4) No junk-value shortcut exists: in my scratch file I proved `series P` is a genuinely summable series under the theorem's hypotheses. (5) A generic-function quantifier example would be a paraphrase, not the file's declaration. No trivial_proof.lean was created, so there is nothing to delete.

submission.summary:
Fixed `Erdos269.erdos_269.variants.rational` by restating it as the exact negation of Erdős's question. Its right-hand side is now `∃ (P : Finset ℕ), (∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) ∧ P.card ≥ 2 ∧ ∃ (q : ℚ), q = (series (P : Set ℕ))`. Before, it was the universal "every such P gives a rational sum", which is neither the source's question nor its negation. The docstring now asks "Is there a finite set of primes P with |P| ≥ 2 for which the sum is rational?" and notes that this negates Erdős's question (`variants.irrational`). The name and `@[category research open, AMS 11]` are unchanged.

Why this fix rather than deletion: my preferred suggestion was to delete the variant and rename `variants.irrational` to `erdos_269`. That needs an edit outside this file, because `FormalConjectures/Subsets/FC100OpenSet1.lean` refers to `Erdos269.erdos_269.variants.rational` via `decl_name%`, which fails the build if the name disappears. Keeping the name and fixing the statement keeps that subset building. Its `verifyCategoryCounts` check still passes, since the category is still `research open`; I confirmed this in a scratch file. If maintainers would rather delete the variant, they must also update FC100OpenSet1.

Checks:
- In a scratch file, the new right-hand side compiles as `↔ ¬` of the right-hand side of `variants.irrational`, so the two answer slots now simply invert.
- The old right-hand side implies the new one.
- The corrected statement is still open. The forum's |P| = 2 transcendence proof no longer settles it, so the status point I raised for this variant no longer applies.

Two trivial docstring/comment edits for the minor item:
- The `series` docstring now says the sum starts at n = 0, whose term 1/lcm(∅) = 1 makes it 1 plus the problem's sum (no effect on rationality).
- The comment in `partialLcm` now reads `{a P 0, ..., a P (n - 1)}`.

No other declaration was touched. The file compiles with only the three `declaration uses 'sorry'` warnings. It is also clean, in both the default and the `postpone` answer modes, with the `FormalConjectures` library's lakefile options (all style linters on, `warn.sorry=false`). `git status` shows `269.lean` as the only file I changed; `lakefile.toml` and `run/` were already modified before I started.

namespace Erdos269
/--
A positive integer $n$ has all its prime factors in the set $P$.
By convention, $1$ satisfies this for any $P$ as it has no prime divisors.

def HasPrimeFactorsIn (P : Set ℕ) (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  n > 0 ∧ ∀ p, p.Prime → p ∣ n → p ∈ P

/--
The infinite, strictly increasing sequence $\{a_0, a_1, \dots\}$ of integers
whose prime factors all belong to $P$.
-/
noncomputable def a (P : Set ℕ) : ℕ → ℕ := Nat.nth <| HasPrimeFactorsIn P

/--
The $n$-th partial least common multiple, $[a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}]$, which is
the LCM of the first $n$ integers in the sequence.
-/
noncomputable def partialLcm (P : Set ℕ) (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  -- We take the LCM of `{a P 0, ..., a P (n - 1)}`.
  (Finset.range n).lcm (a P)

/--
The sum $\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{1}{[a_0,\ldots,a_{n - 1}]}$. Its $n = 0$ term is $1$ (the empty
LCM), so this is $1$ plus the sum in the problem; this does not affect its rationality.
-/
noncomputable def series (P : Set ℕ) : ℝ :=  ∑' n, (1 : ℝ) / (partialLcm P n)

/--
For a set of primes $P$, let $\{a_1 < a_2 < \dots\}$ be the set of positive integers whose
prime factors are all in $P$. Is there a finite set of primes $P$ with $|P| \ge 2$ for which
the sum
$$ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{[a_1,\ldots,a_n]} $$
is rational?

This is the negation of Erdős's question, which asks whether the sum is irrational for every
such $P$ (see `erdos_269.variants.irrational`).
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_269.variants.rational : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ (P : Finset ℕ), (∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) ∧ P.card ≥ 2 ∧
    ∃ (q : ℚ), q = (series (P : Set ℕ)) := by
  sorry

/--
Let $P$ be a finite set of primes with $|P| \ge 2$ and let
$\{a_1 < a_2 < \dots\}$ be the set of positive integers whose prime factors
are all in $P$. Is the sum
$$ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{[a_1,\ldots,a_n]} $$
irrational?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_269.variants.irrational : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ᵉ (P : Finset ℕ) (h : ∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) (h_card : P.card ≥ 2),
    Irrational (series (P : Set ℕ)) := by
  sorry

This theorem addresses the case where the set of primes $P$ is infinite. In this case the sum is
irrational.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_269.variants.infinite (P : Set ℕ) (h : ∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) (h_inf : P.Infinite) :
  Irrational (series P) := by
  sorry

end Erdos269
